title: What Nikole Hannah-Jones Learned from Her Daughter’s School ters-school/
author: Daniel Buck
summary: Daniel Buck summarizes Nikole Hannah-Jones's account of her daughter's schooling as a harrowing record of educational malpractice, from chaotic cafeterias and absent teachers to ungraded math work riddled with errors. He credits her for admitting the mistake and even for wondering whether lowered expectations amount to racism under the guise of antiracism. His critique is that she still will not interrogate the identity-first, antiracist principles that spread through schools after 2020 and undermined grades, homework, honors classes, and discipline. Drawing on his years in urban schools, Buck argues that viewing everything through oppression yields only more funding, excuses, and bureaucracy, while accountability, standards, and discipline never surface. He likens her to a faith healer who admits hand-washing matters but still blames spirits for disease, while welcoming the reckoning her essay may force.
points: Buck highlights the moment Hannah-Jones discovered her daughter's ungraded math work was mostly wrong.
Middle school teachers rewarded problem students for small successes while compliant students went unrecognized.
He argues that antiracist frameworks eliminating grades, homework, honors, and discipline undercut what struggling schools need.
An oppression-only lens, in his experience, produces calls for funding and excuses rather than accountability and standards.
quotes: Much of the essay is a harrowing account of her daughter’s journey through educational malpractice, chronicling the consequences of this decision.

Hannah-Jones is willing to acknowledge her mistake in enrolling Najya in poor-performing schools, and she’s even willing to question if lowered expectations might just amount to “racism under the guise of antiracism.
This analytical framework that subverts standards and rigor—eliminating grades, homework, honors classes, and discipline—undermines everything Hannah-Jones hopes to see in schools.

When the entire system is understood only through a lens in which oppression is the fundamental problem, the “solutions” that emerge are only more funding, more excuses, and more bureaucratic management.
She resembles a faith healer who finally acknowledges that she should have told her subjects to wash their hands, but who still believes that spirits, not germs, cause illness.

The harms caused by nearly a decade of antiracist educational beliefs deserve a reckoning. If Hannah-Jones’s essay forces that conversation, it will prove fruitful despite the harmful ideologies it overlooks.
